messages.author: 00d4a4fc726d0cad
messages.subject: Disperal distance and occupancy models
parts:
So I guess I'll throw in the first question.

I am currently working with a dynamic occupancy model, similar to those in Kery and Schaub 2012 Chapter 13. The occupancy model accounts for both false positives (misclassifications) and false negatives. False positives are a major confounding factor for the population.  I am interested in calculating the probability of colonization (gamma, and possibly persistence, phi) as a function of the distance to other occupied sites. Herein lies the problem. Occupancy is a latent parameter, and is therefore unknown. I have come up with two potential solutions and I could use some help as to how appropriate/inappropriate each solution may be or whether there are alternatives. Ideally, I would like to estimate a probability of colonization based on the minimum distance to an adjacent occupied site. Getting this estimate is going to be somewhat important since there is management occurring that I don’t think we can fairly assess since many nearby sites have become unoccupied and may therefore be unable to be colonized.

Proposed solution 1. I could calculate the distance to each site (fixed point count locations) where unambiguous detections occurred the previous year between each point, resulting in “distance to nearest occupied point” between each year and include this as a covariate for gamma. However this will not appropriately incorporate detectability and adjusted occupancy, so is a little rough.

Proposed solution 2. I would like to use occupancy at t-1, the previous year, influence colonization between years. So I was thinking I model dispersal like this:

Gamma[i,t]<- Beta[0] + Beta[1] *   min(z[ , t-1] * distance matrix[ ,i])  ) + Beta[2] * management[i,t-1] 

Where z is the Bernoulli distributed occupancy and “distance matrix” is matrix estimating the distance between all sites (i by i matrix). I was thinking that I might be able to use z to turn on the sites on the distance matrix that are occupied during the previous year, and turn off the unoccupied sites, thereby regressing the minimum distance to an occupied site for each year. I'm not as familiar with how JAGS works with arrays either, so would multiplying these arrays have the desired effect of turning certain points off that were unoccupied?

Do either of these seem reasonable, or is there another more effective solution? I worry that not accounting for dispersal distance may distort the effects of management.

Thanks in advance for any advice and I'm definitely open to alternatives.

Brian Rolek

Using R, JAGS, jagsUI, on Windows OS

messages.author: 58a62321f08f30f8
messages.subject: RE: Disperal distance and occupancy models
parts:
HI Brian,

 

Might I suggest using a more formal method of accounting for distance – that is, ‘connectivity’.

These paper provide some approaches for calculating connectivity:

http://www.esajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1890/0012-9658(2002)083%5B1131:SCMISE%5D2.0.CO%3B2

 

http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10980-008-9245-4#page-1

 

and this very cool paper (J) outlines a metapopulation model with a dispersal based connectivity component – it has an abundance model that can be removed if you don’t have data on N (Richard Chandler also has a nice paper doing the same with a slightly more elegant formulation of connectivity – perhaps he can pass that along):

 

http://www.esajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0384.1   (pdf available here)

 

Chris

parts:
Thanks Chris. I wouldn't say our model is more elegant by any means, but it is designed specifically for binary data (if that's what you have) and it seems to work well for modeling occupancy dynamics following invasion and/or reintroduction events. The manuscript is in review, but I'll send around a link when/if it gets accepted. 

Richard
